svg.aria-label: Diagram: what Private Google Access actually does in Google Cloud and what its name hides; virtual machine instances that have only internal IP addresses use it to reach the external IP addresses of Google APIs and services, so the privacy is that the traffic stays on Google's network rather than that the endpoint is private, and the configuration requires default routes whose next hop is the default internet gateway; it is enabled subnet by subnet rather than per network, which means two subnets in one network behave differently and legacy networks cannot use it at all because they have no subnets; it has no effect whatsoever on instances that already have an external IP address, since those need no special configuration; the qualifying source addresses are the interface's primary internal IPv4 address, its internal IPv6 address, or an internal IPv4 address from an alias IP range; what it does not cover, namely regional and multi-regional endpoints ending in rep dot googleapis dot com, and services hosted inside VPC networks which need private services access or Private Service Connect instead; and the direct connectivity case where some APIs bypass the Google Front Ends and egress must be allowed to 34.126.0.0/18 and an IPv6 range, needing no DNS records
svg.title: Private Google Access: internal-only VMs reaching external Google addresses, enabled one subnet at a time
svg.text: The name promises a private endpoint. What you get is a private PATH to a public one.
VMs with no external IP reach the EXTERNAL addresses of Google APIs, over Google’s network.
Read the two sentences together and the product makes sense
“VM instances that only have internal IP addresses can use Private Google Access.”
“THEY CAN REACH THE EXTERNAL IP ADDRESSES OF GOOGLE APIS AND SERVICES.”
Hence the configuration everyone double-takes at: you need DEFAULT ROUTES whose NEXT HOP
is DEFAULT-INTERNET-GATEWAY, for 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0. Private access, public destination.
subnet-a — ENABLED
VM A1: internal IP only
→ CAN reach Google APIs
VM A2: has an external IP
→ CAN reach them, but not because
of this setting
Disable it and A1 can only send
subnet-b — NOT ENABLED
VM B1: internal IP only
→ CANNOT reach Google APIs
VM B2: has an external IP
→ CAN reach them anyway — the
setting has NO EFFECT on it
traffic WITHIN the VPC network.
One network, two answers — because the switch is on the SUBNET
“You enable Private Google Access on a subnet by subnet basis; it’s a setting for subnets in
a VPC network.” So an audit that answers at network level answers the wrong question.
Legacy networks cannot use it at all — they have no subnets to set it on.
Which source address qualifies
• The interface’s primary internal IPv4 address
• The interface’s internal IPv6 address
• An internal IPv4 address from an ALIAS IP RANGE — #64’s secondary ranges still count
And the hard precondition: the interface must have NO external IP address assigned.
What it does NOT cover — three different products hide behind one expectation
NOT regional or multi-regional endpoints — anything ending in rep.googleapis.com.
Services published with the Service Networking API → use PRIVATE SERVICES ACCESS.
Services published with Private Service Connect → use PRIVATE SERVICE CONNECT.
It covers Google APIs hosted in Google’s production infrastructure. Not things in VPC networks.
Two operational details that are easy to miss
FIREWALL: the default allow-egress rule already permits this traffic — unless a higher
priority rule blocks it. A tightened egress policy is the usual reason this silently stops working.
DIRECT CONNECTIVITY: some APIs bypass the Google Front Ends entirely. Allow egress to
34.126.0.0/18 (16,384 addresses) and 2001:4860:8040::/42 — and create NO DNS records for them.
WHO CAN TURN IT ON: project owners, editors, and principals with the Network Admin role — the same
people who create and update subnets, because that is what this setting is.
#80’s Network Admin split therefore decides who controls API reachability, not just addressing.
